extracted.intended_audience: legal practitioners, judges, and informed public interested in English bail law
extracted.subtask_description: A historical and legal analysis of English bail law and judicial discretion (statutory and common-law rules governing when prisoners may be admitted to bail). The text surveys statutes, authorities (Blackstone, Hale, Coke), habeas corpus limits, and examples applying principles to a specific case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-bailability of persons taken with the 'maner' (in flagrante delicto)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person positively charged with feloniously stealing, and taken in flagrante delicto, with the stolen goods upon him, is not bailable. The law considers him as differing in nothing from a convict, but in the form of conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly asserted as an obvious legislative meaning and supported by authorities (Blackstone, Hale, Hawkins). Example: when the stolen goods were found upon the thief, bail was refused (Lord Mayor refused to bail John Eyre). The text treats 'taken with the maner' as equivalent to manifest guilt and therefore excluding bail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bail only when it 'stands indifferent' whether guilty or innocent
rubrics_metrics.description: The common practice and allowed general rule is, that bail is only then proper, where it stands indifferent whether the party were guilty or innocent ('quando stat indifferenter').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities (Hale, Coke) repeatedly state bail is appropriate only where guilt is uncertain; when guilt is open and manifest (conviction, confession, or manifest evidence) bail is not proper. The essay cites case examples and doctrinal statements to show this is a controlling evaluative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory prohibitions on bail apply to superior courts unless expressly excepted
rubrics_metrics.description: When the legislature expressly says that any particular offence is by law not bailable, the superior courts are comprehended in the prohibition and bound by it, unless a positive exception of the superior courts exists in the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument traces statutes (Westminster I, later acts) and shows legislature used terms bailable/replevisable synonymously to restrict all bail. Although some commentators argued superior courts were outside statute language, the essay contends the legislative intent was general and binding on all courts; courts should not evade statutory prohibitions by claiming jurisdictional exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction and legislative interchangeability between replevy (sheriffs) and bail (king's bench)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replevy (by sheriffs) and bail (by higher courts) are distinct in law, but the legislature often used the words synonymously and intended the same substantive prohibition (i.e., some offences shall not be 'replevisable' or 'bailable').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Coke's technical distinction is noted, but the statutes' intent (to accept only the body as security for certain offences) means the practical effect is to forbid enlargement by security regardless of which officer or court acts. The essay cites authorities to show terms were used promiscuously and argues for interpreting statutes by purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habeas Corpus Act (31 Charles II) exclusions and procedural limits on bail
rubrics_metrics.description: The Habeas Corpus Act particularly declares that it is not meant to extend to treason or felony plainly and specially expressed in the warrant of commitment; in such cases the prisoner is left to seek remedy at common law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The act also requires judges, on motion in open court the last day of term/sessions, to either set the prisoner at liberty on bail unless it appears by oath that witnesses for the king could not be produced that term. The essay emphasizes the act's terms are enacting (creating limits where none before) and that procedural timing and express wording in warrants matter for bail eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of expressing reason on every commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is absolutely necessary to express, upon every commitment, the reason for which it is made, so that on a Habeas Corpus the court may examine its validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to state cause may enable perpetual imprisonment; expressing cause allows the court to discharge, admit to bail, or remand according to the circumstances. Blackstone and other authorities are cited to support this procedural requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment for granting bail contrary to law
rubrics_metrics.description: If bail be granted otherwise than the law alloweth, the party that alloweth the same shall be fined, imprisoned, render damages, or forfeit his place, as the case shall require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule (cited from Selden) is presented as a deterrent and enforces that magistrates and judges who improperly grant bail are subject to penalties; the essay uses it to argue against arbitrary judicial enlargement of prisoners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited authority of justices of the peace to bail (historical statutory limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justices of the peace were at one time empowered to bail persons arrested on light suspicion of felony, but subsequent statutes (e.g., 3 Henry VII) limited this power (requiring two justices, one of quorum), and later statutes removed power to bail for offences declared not bailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text traces how legislative responses to abuses repeatedly restricted local magistrates' power to let prisoners to bail or mainprize; historical reforms were motivated by abuses where single justices released notable offenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts may consider particular circumstances to grant bail despite general prohibition, but discretion must not be arbitrary
rubrics_metrics.description: Although statutes declare some offences irreplevisable, superior courts in their discretion may admit bail when particular favourable circumstances render it doubtful whether the prisoner is guilty; such latitude is for circumstances inductive of doubt, not arbitrary preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay criticizes any exercise of discretion that ignores statutory rules and warns that treating judicial latitude as an absolute power to bail in all cases would be a violation of the law. Examples and debate (Blackstone, Selden) illustrate permissible vs. impermissible discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition extends to all means that accomplish the forbidden result
rubrics_metrics.description: When any thing is forbidden, all the means by which the same thing may be compassed or done are equally forbidden ('quando aliquid prohibetur, prohibetur et omne per quod devenitur ad illud').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a principle of statutory construction: if the legislature forbids enlargement for certain offences, courts may not evade that prohibition by using different procedural devices or forum differences to achieve the same end of releasing prisoners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of being 'taken with vert or venison' to indictment in forest offences
rubrics_metrics.description: In offences relating to the forest, if a man was taken with vert or venison, it was declared to be equivalent to indictment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historical statutory example is cited to show earlier conceptions of 'taken with' as conferring the same immediate consequence as formal indictment, supporting the non-bailability rule for persons taken in such circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notoriously guilty persons, outlaws, or attainted are not bailable
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlaws, persons attainted upon their own confession, notorious felons, and those clearly defeasible by statute are declared not bailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations (Blackstone, Hale, Hawkins) list categories of persons not to be admitted to bail; the essay uses these classifications to argue the defendant in the case falls into a non-bailable category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts must judge sufficiency of the habeas return and act accordingly (discharge, bail, or remand)
rubrics_metrics.description: The court, upon view of the return, judgeth of the sufficiency or insufficiency of it. If they think the prisoner in law to be bailable, he is committed to the marshal and bailed; if not, he is remanded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The procedural test on habeas corpus is whether cause of commitment is lawful and sufficient; if lawful, remand; if unlawful, discharge; if doubtful, bail; authorities (Hale, Lord Chief Justice Hyde) illustrate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habeas corpus relief and bail only when temporary enlargement causes no inconvenience to public justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Habeas Corpus Act extends only to the case of commitments for such criminal charge as can produce no inconvenience to public justice by a temporary enlargement of the prisoner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges must weigh 'the quality of the prisoner and nature of the offence' when deciding bail under habeas; the act allows bail only where temporary release will not prejudice public justice (explicit statutory limitation).
